User: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Seattle WA. W-2 from Acme Corp: $82,350. Side income: $11,200 from web design (3 clients). Interest $2,340 (Chase savings), dividends $550 (Interactive Brokers). Home office: 155 sq ft, rent $1,820/month, apartment 680 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,400 (Sallie Mae, 2019–2020); charity $2,000 to Boston Medical Center (donation, have receipt) with receipt; unreimbursed expenses $720. Can you help me fig

ure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
Assistant: Thanks—here’s how this shakes out based on what you shared.

Bottom line
- Standard vs itemized: Take the standard deduction for 2024. For MFJ it’s $29,200, which far exceeds your likely itemizable amounts (mainly $2,000 charity; WA has no state income tax and you’re renting, so SALT/itemized totals would still be far below $29,200).
- Home office: You likely qualify as self-employed (web design). Your off

ice is 155 sq ft out of 680 sq ft (≈22.8%). With rent of $1,820/month ($21,840/yr):
  - Simplified method: 155 × $5 = $775.
  - Actual method (rent only): 22.8% × $21,840 ≈ $4,980. This is much larger and can be deducted on Schedule C (limited to business profit; any excess may carry forward). You don’t file Form 8829 if you use the simplified method; you do file Form 8829 if using actual expenses.
- Student loan interest: You can deduct up to $2,500 above-the-line on Schedule 1. Your income is well below t

he phaseout, so you should get the full $2,500 (even though you paid $4,400).
- Unreimbursed expenses ($720): 
  - If these are employee (W-2) job expenses, they’re not deductible for federal 2024.
  - If they’re business expenses for your web design work, deduct them on Schedule C (not as itemized deductions).

Key estimates (rough, for planning)
- Schedule C net profit after actual-method home office: $11,200 − ~$4,980 ≈ $6,220 (before any other business expenses).
- Self-employment tax on that profit: ≈

$880; half of this (≈ $440) is an above-the-line deduction.
- AGI ballpark:
  - Income: $82,350 (W-2) + ~$6,220 (Sched C) + $2,340 (interest) + $550 (dividends) ≈ $91,460
  - Adjustments: −$2,500 (student loan interest) − ~$440 (half SE tax) ≈ −$2,940
  - AGI ≈ $88,520
- Taxable income after standard deduction: ~$88,520 − $29,200 ≈ $59,320
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: likely available; roughly 20% of QBI (about $1,100 based on these estimates). Claimed on Form 8995. This reduces taxable inco

me further.

Which forms you’ll use
- Form 1040 (MFJ)
- Schedule 1: 
  - Part I for business income flowing from Schedule C
  - Part II for adjustments, including student loan interest and half of SE tax
- Schedule C: Report web design income and expenses (include home office; plus any other business costs like supplies, software, a business share of internet, etc.)
- Form 8829: Only if using the actual home office method. If using the simplified method, use the worksheet and report on Schedule C (no 8829).

- Schedule SE: Self-employment tax
- Form 8995: Qualified Business Income deduction (simple version, assuming eligibility)
- Schedule B: Interest and dividends (interest > $1,500 triggers Schedule B)

Notes and tips
- Home office eligibility: Space must be used regularly and exclusively for the business and be your principal place of business (or a place where you meet clients). If you also have utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., those can be included under the actual method (allocated by the same %).
-

Report all side income even if you don’t receive 1099 forms from clients.
- Dividends: Some may be qualified and get favorable rates; you’ll determine that from your 1099-DIV.
- Washington state: No state income tax return.

Open questions to confirm
- Are the $720 unreimbursed expenses related to your W-2 job or your web design business?
- Do you have any other business expenses (software, domain/hosting, equipment, part of internet/phone, supplies)? If yes, we can add those to Schedule C and refine the nu

mbers.
- Do you want to use the actual home office method (larger deduction, more recordkeeping) or the simplified method (smaller but easy)?

If you’d like, I can turn this into a step-by-step checklist and a tighter estimate once you confirm those details.
